keyVerseText: And they had a king over them, which is the angel of the bottomless pit, whose name in the Hebrew tongue is Abaddon, but in the Greek tongue hath his name Apollyon. Apollyon: that is to say, A destroyer
rootMeaning: The word Ἀπολλύων (Apollyon) is derived as the active participle of the Greek verb ἀπόλλυμι (apóllymi), which means to destroy fully, perish, or lose. This root conveys an active, ongoing process of destruction or ruin, rather than a mere event or title. Understanding Apollyon as 'the destroyer' emphasizes the inherent nature of the one so named as continuously engaged in the act of bringing about loss or ruin, which enriches the common English gloss by highlighting the dynamic and persistent aspect of destruction.
usageInScripture: This term appears only once in Scripture, specifically in Revelation 9:11, where it is used as a proper name for the angel of the bottomless pit. The translation consistently renders Ἀπολλύων as 'Apollyon,' directly linking the name to the concept of destruction. This singular usage underscores the uniqueness and significance of this figure as the embodiment of destruction, rather than a generic descriptor, reinforcing the weight of the title within the apocalyptic context.
theologicalSignificance: Theologically, the name Apollyon reveals profound truths about the nature of evil and spiritual opposition in Scripture. As 'the destroyer,' this figure personifies the destructive power that opposes God's kingdom and seeks to undo His purposes. Recognizing Apollyon as an active agent of destruction calls believers to understand the seriousness of spiritual warfare and the reality of satanic opposition. Yet, in the Christian faith, this destructive power is ultimately subject to the sovereign authority of Christ, who conquers all enemies. Thus, the name Apollyon serves as a solemn reminder of the destructive forces at work but also points believers toward the hope and victory found in Christ.
keyVerseReflection: Revelation 9:11 introduces Apollyon as the king of the locust-like beings released from the abyss, describing him as 'the angel of the bottomless pit' whose Greek name means 'A destroyer.' This explicit identification highlights the destructive role he plays within the vision. The use of the name Apollyon in this verse deepens the understanding of the angel’s character, portraying him not merely as a ruler but as one whose essence is destruction, which aligns with the Hebrew name Abaddon. This dual naming emphasizes the fearful reality of judgment and destruction in the apocalyptic narrative.
